name: 卸）神保町食肉センター 本店 (Jimbocho Shokuniku Center (Honten))

claims.text: Meat is cooked on shared tabletop yakiniku grills alongside items brushed with soy-sauce-based tare, creating likely cross-contact for gluten-sensitive/celiac diners; no dedicated gluten-free grill or preparation area was found in any source.

The restaurant's tare-marinated cuts follow standard yakiniku practice using soy sauce, which in Japan is typically wheat-based unless specified otherwise; no wheat-free soy sauce or tamari alternative was mentioned in any source.
Some cuts (liver, heart, some pork/beef) are offered plain with salt (shio) rather than tare, which structurally avoids the soy-sauce marinade if requested.

No explicit statement was found about the wheat content of the tare/soy sauce used, but standard Japanese yakitori tare and oden broth typically contain wheat-based soy sauce, so this should be assumed present unless staff confirm otherwise.
No dedicated gluten-free preparation area, protocol, or wheat-free noodle guarantee has been documented; this is a shared traditional kitchen that also fries wheat-battered tempura.
The dipping sauce and dashi follow standard Edo-style soba preparation (bonito dashi with soy sauce); no wheat-free tamari or gluten-free sauce alternative was mentioned in any source found.
Dashi is made with dried bonito (katsuobushi), and the menu includes tempura and sashimi, so the kitchen is not set up for vegan cooking; no plant-based dashi option was found in any source.
Uses domestically grown buckwheat, stone-ground on the premises each morning for freshly milled noodles.

name: 小料理屋 さと (Koryoriya Sato)

claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free process documented; kitchen prepares a wheat-gluten (fu) dish as a signature item, indicating no separation of gluten-containing ingredients.

Small, single-proprietress kitchen where every dish is made to order/by hand, which could in principle allow a dish to be discussed and adjusted if asked directly in Japanese — but this is not a documented policy, only an inference from the restaurant's small scale.

name: クンバ ドゥ ファラフェル (Kuumba du Falafel)

claims.text: No source found addressing whether falafel is fried in a fryer shared with wheat-breaded items; not confirmed either way.
Falafel (the core protein) is chickpea-based and inherently free of animal products and gluten before assembly into the wheat-pita sandwich.

name: Sumatra Curry Kyoeido (スマトラカレー 共栄堂)

claims.text: Century-old single-item curry counter with no stated allergen protocol; sauce is flour-free by recipe but the kitchen is shared and residual cross-contact is not controlled.
Each meat is simmered in a different bouillon base: 「具材ごとにカレーソースのベースとなるブイヨンを変え、別々に煮込んでいる」 — an unverified potential wheat source not covered by the no-flour claim.
claims.source: https://kanda-curry.com/共栄堂/ (via WebSearch summary; also san-tatsu.jp/articles/146795, mononcle.jp/column/aji-no-maestro/11768)

claims.text: The 'no wheat flour' statement is scoped only to the sauce roux: 「濃褐色のソースは、小麦粉を一切使わず、20数種類の香辛料を1時間かけてじっくり炒めて作ります」 — no allergen or cross-contamination assurance.
The potage soup is confirmed as a complimentary service to cool the palate, not a GF-verified item: 「サービスでポタージュスープをお出ししており…」 — likely flour-thickened, correctly flagged skip.

AI-generated allergen listings for the shop flag celery and warn they may contain errors, underscoring there is no authoritative allergen data: 'allergen information lists celery... powered by AI and may contain errors, so you should always check with your server.'
No FindMeGlutenFree or HappyCow celiac reviews exist for the shop — targeted search returned no results, so there is no independent celiac corroboration.

The fukujinzuke pickle served with curry is typically seasoned with wheat-based soy sauce; request the curry without it. The spice sauce itself is described as flour-free but the shop makes no tamari claim, so confirm no wheat soy in the masala if pressed.
Not applicable — all curries are meat/seafood based; no vegan menu.
No allergy-handling or gluten-free program is advertised; this is a traditional counter shop, so a celiac must rely on the naturally flour-free recipe plus their own topping/soup avoidance.
Shop explicitly cooks its dark curry sauce with no wheat flour — 「小麦粉を一切使わず、20数種類の香辛料を1時間かけて炒めて作ります」 — the key reason a flour-roux dish like Japanese curry becomes possible for a celiac here.
Curry is served over plain premium Koshihikari rice, which is naturally gluten-free.

Noodles are 十割 (juwari) — 100% stone-ground buckwheat with no wheat flour mixed in — but no gluten-free protocol, allergen statement, or dedicated fryer was found in any source; tempura is on the menu, which typically involves a wheat-flour batter and shared fryer oil in traditional soba kitchens.
No source found describes the tsuyu (dipping sauce) recipe or confirms a bonito-free dashi option; traditional Edo-style soba tsuyu is generally dashi-based.
Buckwheat is sourced directly from named growers in Niigata and Nagano and stone-milled fresh in-house daily using multiple traditional stone mills, rather than using pre-milled commercial flour.

name: 京都 茶寮翠泉 新宿店 (Kyoto Saryo Suisen Shinjuku)

claims.text: The soba dipping sauce (tsuyu) ingredients are not specified in any source found; standard Japanese soba tsuyu is made with wheat-containing soy sauce, but this has not been confirmed for this shop specifically.
The house soba (including the signature matcha soba) is made in-house daily as 十割そば — 100% buckwheat flour with no wheat flour used as a binder in the noodle itself.
